en: *Tattvaratnāvaloka* (Tra). Om. Homage to the feet of the venerable True Guru!
Śrīnivāsa, whose nature is incomparable bliss, who is without abode, who possesses the knowledge of the forms of the ten peerless goddesses, and who is endowed with wisdom;
Victorious is the lotus-handed one, free from change, who brings about the attainment of welfare and happiness for the three worlds, as long as the quarters of space remain in bloom.
Those who do not clearly understand the nature of the fourth consecration, which is contained within the beautiful system of the glorious Mantra-nīti and is devoid of explicit words—
for their clear comprehension, an effort is made through the sevenfold divisions crowded with various collections of instructions.

For all the non-Buddhist teachers are indeed confused in their understanding regarding the knowledge of the nature of reality and that which is to be realized; thus there is a popular saying among people that the Vedāntin is the knower of reality who excels over them. (Tra 3)
The Vedāntins desire as the goal that which is of the nature of bliss, unshakable by its own cognition, and peaceful;
while the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Jinas desire as their goal the cessation of the substrate consisting of form and the other aggregates.
It is empty of [conceptual] forms, having the nature of the moon in the sky, to be personally realized, and possessing the essence of compassion;
it is adorned with the excellent marks, performs the welfare of others, is the natural outflow of generosity and the other perfections, and is free from [worldly] pleasure.
They declare that the goal to be accomplished is one whose limbs are adorned with the marks of blissful existence, who is being enjoyed by those established on the ten stages,
who acts for the benefit of sentient beings, and who abides in the method of the six perfections beginning with generosity.
Having fulfilled all qualities such as generosity without exception, having awakened to them, and having performed every duty,
that which is the direct realization of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)— that too exists in the form of cessation.
They proclaim the goal to be that which embraces its own limbs, which effects its own purpose, which has the nature of liberation from both sufferings and pleasures,
whose body is adorned with the eighty secondary marks, and which is free from conceptual construction.

Having first conceived that which is devoid of the specific form of one's own deity as being clearly manifest bliss, someone declared it to be called "Great Bliss" (mahāsukha), which accomplishes the welfare of the world like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi). (Tra 9)
Having directly visualized one's own lord as having a pleasant form, and subsequently abandoning that mere pleasantness, the fruit will be attained.
Since it is not possible to make [the deity] pure and manifest [in that way], the aspect of one's own lord is thus cultivated.

Another proclaims that the goal to be realized is empty of annihilation— a body equal to space, its limbs adorned with the marks [of a great man], filled with incomparable bliss, united with its own nature, and radiating as the immeasurable Lord of Sages who acts for the benefit of all sentient beings.

Having made one's own lord manifest in a pleasant form, the result would be the mere knowledge of equanimity—a state that remains until the end of saṃsāra, performs the welfare of sentient beings, resembles a wish-fulfilling jewel, and is exclusively peaceful. // Tra_12 //
Having manifested the maṇḍala in its pleasant form, he subsequently attains nirvāṇa according to his own will;
for there is no absence of the welfare of sentient beings in this case, since their manifestation arises from one who has attained nirvāṇa.
Having clearly manifested their desired form, someone later declares cessation as the result;
since cessation is of an undifferentiated nature, there is no distinction in it despite the difference in [the proponents'] positions.
Beyond the knowledge of wisdom (prajñājñāna) is the tasting of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), which is the fourth state; it is the remainder,
the great enclosure,
because every effort in meditations becomes useless once that fruit has been attained and established.
The fourth consecration is said to be the experience of the taste of the consort (rāmā) attained subsequent to the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*);
it is considered inferior because all effort previously applied toward cultivation and so forth is rendered fruitless and becomes merely an attachment.
O Knower of the Lotus purified by the Vedic thunderbolt-seed,
you cause the sprout of existence to flourish and bring the fourth grain to full maturity.
Though manifest, it remains hidden even from the wise.

The five lamps, the drops of nectar, the moon, and the mandalas arising from the drop between the eyebrows are the true nature of the wind; as for the uvula and so forth, which are not the true nature, they are to be inferred by oneself.
Like a dream, a magician’s trick, a reflection, an illusion, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, the moon in water,
and all other things expressible by way of analogy, there is nothing else here to be accomplished that has not already been stated.

One should not entertain delusions regarding other beings who are to be accomplished, using words that are profound, empty, mere appearances, peaceful, extremely subtle, and inexpressible, or such terms as "unstained," "formless," and "untainted."
The *Tattvaratnāvaloka* is completed.
This work is by the venerable scholar Vāgīśvarakīrti.
